# Ambient simplices: lattice-count marginals and exact slice/cap calculus

This note treats actual ambient simplices, keeping the integer base
coordinates fixed. It supplies a lattice-count normal form in all
integer dimensions, exact one-base slice and moment formulas with
repeated height knots, and a cap formula retaining the actual common
halfspace. An explicit six-dimensional simplex then shows that its
projected mixed law need not be logconcave and need not satisfy the
ordinary Gamma_5 centroid halfspace inequality.

The example has three positive integer fibers, different endpoint
simplexes and a nonsimplex middle fiber. Its mixed true centroid has
integer base. It is nevertheless safely above its mixed OC target at
an explicitly specified middle-fiber centroid. No reduction of OC to
ambient simplices is asserted.

All mixed measures in this note use full d-dimensional fiber volume.
Normalized depth or a mixed centroid is asserted only when their total
mass is positive. A full ambient simplex can instead have only
lower-dimensional sampled fibers; no intrinsic H_q weight transfer for
q<d is claimed by the constant d-dimensional Jacobian below.

## 1. A base-preserving barycentric normal form in all dimensions

Let C be a full-dimensional (n+d)-simplex in R^n x R^d, d>=1.
Choose n+1 vertices whose base projections are affinely independent,
and let Q be their n-simplex of base projections. Such a selection
exists because C is full dimensional. Denote the base projections of
the remaining d vertices by h_1,...,h_d. Keep the original base z,
and use their d barycentric coordinates x_1,...,x_d as the new
continuous coordinates. Put S=sum x_j.

This is an invertible affine change of ambient coordinates. Indeed,
a kernel vector has all remaining barycentric variations zero;
the selected n+1 variations have sum zero and base moment zero.
Their affine independence makes all of them zero. The map keeps z
EXACTLY unchanged, so it preserves Z^n x R^d.

The image simplex is precisely
\[
 {\cal C}=\{(z,x):x\in T_d,\quad
 z\in \sum_{j=1}^d h_jx_j+(1-S)Q\},\qquad
 T_d=\{x\ge0:S\le1\}.                                \tag{1}
\]
Its ordinary ambient volume is
\[
 |{\cal C}|=|Q|\int_{T_d}(1-S)^n\,dx
             =\frac{n!\,|Q|}{(n+d)!}.               \tag{2}
\]
The last elementary simplex integral follows by successive
integration, or the beta integral. Hence the constant absolute
continuous-fiber Jacobian of the coordinate map is
\[
              J=\frac{n!\,|Q|}{(n+d)!\,|C|}.        \tag{3}
\]
The ambient derivative has block form [[I,0],[*,A]], so its determinant
is exactly the continuous-fiber determinant det A. Thus every mixed
mass and every ambient cap mass is multiplied by the same J.
Normalized depths, admissible integer bases, and affine centroids
are transported exactly for this positive full-d-volume measure.
No affine change of the integer lattice
has been hidden in this normalization.

The projected mixed measure on T_d has the EXACT density
\[
 N(x)=\#\left(\mathbb Z^n\cap
        \left[\sum_jh_jx_j+(1-S)Q\right]\right).      \tag{4}
\]
Brackets here denote the displayed closed convex set, not coordinate
rounding. Formula (4) follows by summing its fiber indicators. It
includes boundary lattice points. Any ambiguities of density on the
boundary S=1 are immaterial for d-volume, while individual closed
ambient cap boundaries are handled before projection.

For n=1, choose the two extreme vertex heights a<b. If the remaining
heights are h_j, (1) reads
\[
 x\in T_d,\quad
 \ell(x)=a+\sum_j(h_j-a)x_j\le z
 \le u(x)=b+\sum_j(h_j-b)x_j,                         \tag{5}
\]
with u(x)-ell(x)=(b-a)(1-S). The density is
\[
 \max\{0,\ \lfloor u(x)\rfloor-\lceil\ell(x)\rceil+1\}.
\]
The affine phase ell(x), as well as the shrinking width, is retained.
For n=0, the same statement uses a point Q, 0!=|Q|_0=1 and the count
one; it reduces to the ordinary simplex normal form.

## 2. One integer coordinate: knots and ordinary slice density

Return to the original coordinates of an actual (d+1)-simplex C.
Write m=d+1, N=d+2, and its vertices as
\[
             v_i=(h_i,\xi_i),\qquad 0\le i<N.
\]
The heights are not all equal. Let w(s) be the d-volume of its
continuous fiber at base s, and let V=|C| be its ambient volume.

For distinct heights and min h_i<s<max h_i,
\[
 w(s)=V\,m\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}
              \frac{(h_i-s)_+^{m-1}}
                   {\prod_{j\ne i}(h_i-h_j)}.        \tag{6}
\]
For repeated heights, the precise version is the confluent divided
difference
\[
       w(s)=V\,m\,[h_0,\ldots,h_{N-1}]
                              (t-s)_+^{m-1}.       \tag{7}
\]
The divided difference is in the variable t. At an interior knot,
(7) is defined by its continuous s-limit if necessary. Equivalently,
combine repeated nodes by the usual Hermite derivatives away from
their kink. Do not replace those derivatives at an extreme kink by
an arbitrary one-sided convention.

Here is a proof that also fixes the normalization. Uniform barycentric
coordinates of a simplex have density m! on
Delta_m={lambda_i>=0, sum lambda_i=1}, using m independent coordinates.
For a smooth f the elementary Hermite--Genocchi identity is
\[
 [h_0,\ldots,h_m]f
      =\int_{\Delta_m}f^{(m)}\left(\sum_i h_i\lambda_i\right)d\lambda.
                                                               \tag{8}
\]
It follows inductively from the divided-difference recursion:
integrating the lambda_m derivative of f^(m-1) gives the two faces
lambda_0=0 and lambda_m=0, and a factor h_m-h_0.
Repeated nodes follow by continuity.

Use f(t)=(t-s)_+^m, justified by smooth approximation. Its m-th
derivative is m! times the upper-halfline indicator almost everywhere.
Therefore the upper tail of H=sum h_i lambda_i is exactly
\[
 {\mathbb P}(H\ge s)
             =[h_0,\ldots,h_m](t-s)_+^m.             \tag{9}
\]
The event H=s has ordinary ambient volume zero because H is
nonconstant. Differentiating (9) in s gives (6)-(7).
The ambient-coordinate coarea factor is one because z is the first
Euclidean coordinate. In particular int w(s) ds=V.

### Closed endpoint fibers and repeated knots

Define w(s)=0 outside [h_min,h_max]. At an endpoint define its value
as the ONE-SIDED LIMIT FROM INSIDE this interval. This equals the
actual closed fiber volume. Indeed, the compact fibers converge in
Hausdorff distance to the endpoint face by convex interpolation,
and their d-volume converges to that face's d-volume.

If k vertices attain an extreme height, its face has dimension k-1.
It has positive d-volume exactly when k=d+1=m; otherwise w is zero
at that endpoint. This possible positive endpoint value must be
included in a sampled sum over integer bases.

For example, heights 0 repeated m times and 1 once give
\[
 w(s)=mV(1-s)^{m-1}\quad(0\le s\le1).
\]
Thus w(0)=mV>0. The formula with m repeats of the kink at zero is
not evaluated by assigning a classical derivative to
(t-0)_+^(m-1) there. Likewise, m repeats of the maximum use the
left endpoint limit. These conventions avoid losing a whole
positive-volume integer boundary fiber.

## 3. Exact section centroids and sampled moments

Let f_h=w/V denote the normalized scalar density in Section 2.
Let h^(i) be the knot multiset with one additional copy of h_i, and
let f_{h^(i)} be the scalar density for uniform barycentrics on that
larger simplex. Then the unnormalized barycentric moment profile is
\[
 J_i(s):=\int_{C_s}\lambda_i(s,x)\,dx
       =\frac V N\,f_{h^{(i)}}(s)
       =V[h_0,\ldots,h_{N-1},h_i](t-s)_+^m.          \tag{10}
\]
The same interior limits and closed endpoint rules apply.

To prove (10), merge two uniform-simplex barycentric coordinates
whose heights both equal h_i. For fixed merged coordinate lambda_i,
the splitting interval has length lambda_i. Thus the merged law
has density N lambda_i times the original uniform barycentric law.
This is the elementary Dirichlet (2,1,...,1) identity and proves
(10), including its factor 1/N. No unknown normalization is hidden
in the duplicated-knot formula.

Whenever w(s)>0, the ACTUAL ordinary centroid of that fiber is
\[
                  g(s)=\frac{\sum_i J_i(s)v_i}{w(s)}.           \tag{11}
\]
Its base coordinate is s. The identities
\[
 \sum_i J_i(s)=w(s),\qquad \sum_i h_iJ_i(s)=s\,w(s)
\]
also follow directly from barycentric coordinates.
For the mixed source,
\[
 M=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}w(j),\qquad
 \bar\lambda_i=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}J_i(j)}M.    \tag{12}
\]
All sums are finite and retain the endpoint values from Section 2.
The mixed true centroid is sum bar-lambda_i v_i. Its base need not
be integral; it is an admissible mixed candidate only when it is
integral. Formula (11), by contrast, always supplies an admissible
point at every positive INTEGER fiber.

## 4. Canonical vertex caps: an exact sampled formula

For 0<=c<1, the entire closed ambient cap lambda_i>=c is the simplex
\[
                   cv_i+(1-c)C.
\]
At an integer base j its fiber is the continuous homothetic image
of the original fiber at
s=(j-c h_i)/(1-c). Consequently
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \mu_C\{\lambda_i\ge c\}
   =(1-c)^d\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}
           w\left(\frac{j-c h_i}{1-c}\right).\quad}  \tag{13}
\]
For c=1 the cap is a vertex and has mixed d-volume zero (d>=1);
larger c also gives zero, and c<0 gives the whole source.
Formula (13) tracks the original integer bases j: the transformed
arguments of w are real and are NOT rounded.

It includes vertical canonical caps. If all vertices other than i
have one common height, lambda_i is a function of z alone. A cap
boundary may then contain a whole positive d-volume fiber; its
mass is preserved by the closed endpoint convention in (13).

The exact cap through the mixed true centroid, if that centroid is
admissible, uses c=bar-lambda_i from (12). Through the own centroid
of fiber j it uses c=J_i(j)/w(j). These are actual ambient halfspace
tests, not cap fractions assigned independently to the fibers.

## 5. Arbitrary cap directions via a projective product

There is also an exact formula retaining one arbitrary shared cap.
Fix a non-knot s strictly between the extreme heights, and split
I={i:h_i<s}, J={j:h_j>s}. Set delta_i=|h_i-s|.
Let alpha lie in Delta_{|I|-1}, beta in Delta_{|J|-1}, using ordinary
simplex-coordinate measures of total masses 1/(|I|-1)! and
1/(|J|-1)! (Delta_0 has mass one). Put
\[
 L(\alpha,\beta)=
       \sum_{i\in I}\frac{\alpha_i}{\delta_i}
             +\sum_{j\in J}\frac{\beta_j}{\delta_j}.
\]
The barycentric section is parametrized by
\[
 \lambda_i=\frac{\alpha_i}{\delta_i L}\ (i\in I),
 \qquad
 \lambda_j=\frac{\beta_j}{\delta_j L}\ (j\in J).       \tag{14}
\]
This is a bijection of relative interiors. The constraints
sum lambda=1 and sum h lambda=s follow immediately; conversely
delta_i lambda_i on the two sides have the same sum, which
recovers alpha and beta.

The exact section-volume formula is
\[
 w(s)=\frac{m!V}{\prod_i\delta_i}
    \int_{\Delta_{|I|-1}\times\Delta_{|J|-1}}
                      L^{-m}\,d\alpha\,d\beta.      \tag{15}
\]
For a closed ambient affine cap whose vertex values are a_i and
whose threshold is b, insert into the integrand the indicator
\[
 \sum_{i\in I}\frac{(a_i-b)\alpha_i}{\delta_i}
 +\sum_{j\in J}\frac{(a_j-b)\beta_j}{\delta_j}\ge0.    \tag{16}
\]
Thus the cap inequality becomes ONE linear inequality on the
product, while the density is the negative power of ONE positive
affine function. There is no loss of cap coupling.

For completeness, the Jacobian can be obtained directly from
barycentric Fubini. Substitute u_i=delta_i lambda_i on the lower
side and v_j=delta_j lambda_j on the upper side. Their sums must
agree. Write u=t alpha and v=t beta. The product-simplex
Jacobians contribute t^(|I|-1)t^(|J|-1); the remaining sum-lambda
constraint is tL=1, whose one-dimensional Jacobian is 1/L.
Their product is L^-(N-1)=L^-m. The original barycentric
ambient Jacobian is m!V, and the coordinate scaling contributes
1/product delta_i, giving (15). Equivalently this computation
can be integrated against a test function of s before taking the
slice, so it does not assume a formal Dirac delta identity.

At an interior height knot take the continuous slice limit for
a NONVERTICAL cap. Compact convex fibers converge in Hausdorff
distance, and the cap boundary is d-volume null, so dominated
convergence gives the correct cap value. The same one-sided rule
works at an endpoint. For a VERTICAL cap do not replace the closed
boundary mass by a limiting convention: its contribution is
exactly w(j) times its closed integer-base indicator. This treats
the only possibility of a cap boundary carrying full fiber volume.

## 6. A nonhomothetic ambient-simplex family

Fix d>=2 and 0<epsilon<1. In the normal coordinates of (5), take
the d+2 vertices
\[
 (0,0),\ (4,0),\ (2-\epsilon,e_1),\
 (2+\epsilon,e_2),\ (2,e_3),\ldots,(2,e_d).           \tag{17}
\]
They are affinely independent. The ambient volume is 4/(d+1)!.
There are five distinct vertex heights (four when d=2), so this
is not a two-height product model. The only positive integer
fibers are at bases 1,2,3. The extreme integer fibers at 0 and 4
are singletons and have zero d-volume.

Write V_T=|T_d|=1/d!. The fibers are
\[
 \begin{split}
 A_\epsilon&=\operatorname{diag}\big(
 (2-\epsilon)^{-1},(2+\epsilon)^{-1},1/2,\ldots,1/2\big)T_d,\\
 B_\epsilon&=\{x\ge0:2\sum x_i+
                                  \epsilon|x_1-x_2|\le2\},\\
 C_\epsilon&=\text{the coordinate swap }x_1\leftrightarrow x_2
                                          \text{ of }A_\epsilon .
 \end{split}                                                   \tag{18}
\]
These follow directly from the two affine inequalities (5).
For the base-one fiber the other inequality is redundant because
epsilon<1; the base-three statement follows by reflection.
Thus the hull completion and the absence of further positive
integer fibers have been checked, not postulated.

Relative to V_T their volumes are
\[
 a=\frac{2^{2-d}}{4-\epsilon^2},\qquad
 W=\frac2{2+\epsilon},\qquad a.                      \tag{19}
\]
For the middle formula, start with T_d and remove the two disjoint
vertex caps cut by 2 sum x ± epsilon(x_1-x_2)>2.
Each removed simplex has volume fraction
epsilon/[2(2+epsilon)]: its edge ratios at the apex are
epsilon/(2+epsilon), 1/2, and d-2 copies of 1.
For epsilon>0 the endpoint simplexes are not positively homothetic
and the middle is not a simplex. This is a genuine ambient-simplex
source beyond the homothetic roof-chain class.

### Failure of projected logconcavity

The projected density is the lattice count from (5). At points
x_s=(s/d,...,s/d), the height interval is [2s,4-2s].
For s=2/5,3/5,4/5 the density values are respectively 3,1,1.
The middle point is the midpoint of the other two, and
\[
                         1<\sqrt{3\cdot1}.
\]
All three points are interior to T_d and their counts persist on
open neighborhoods. Therefore no change on a null set can make
this density logconcave. An ordinary logconcave-marginal theorem
cannot be applied merely from ambient convexity.

## 7. An admissible true-centroid obstruction in dimension five

The transformation (z,x_1,x_2,x_3,...) ->
(4-z,x_2,x_1,x_3,...) preserves the simplex and its mixed measure.
Its true mixed centroid therefore has base 2 and x_1=x_2.
It lies in the positive middle fiber and is an admissible point.

Let q be the sum of its continuous coordinates. Elementary simplex
moments in (18) give
\[
 q=\frac{
 W\left(d-\frac{\epsilon}{2+\epsilon}\right)
 +2a\left(\frac d2+\frac{\epsilon^2}{4-\epsilon^2}\right)}
 {(d+1)(W+2a)}.                                     \tag{20}
\]
For the middle, each removed cap has one vertex with sum coordinate
2/(2+epsilon) and d vertices with sum coordinate one. This proves
its moment in (20); the endpoint moments follow by summing their
axis lengths.

If
\[
             \frac1{2-\epsilon}<q<\frac2{2+\epsilon},             \tag{21}
\]
the actual closed cylindrical cap sum x_i<=q contains both endpoint
fibers entirely. Its intersection with the middle is exactly qT_d:
for x in qT_d,
2 sum x+epsilon|x_1-x_2|<=(2+epsilon)q<2.
Thus this through-centroid cap has mass
\[
                       (q^d+2a)V_T.                \tag{22}
\]

Take d=5 and epsilon=1/10. Then, exactly,
\[
 a=25/798,\quad W=20/21,\quad W+2a=135/133,\quad
 q=310337/387828.
\]
Condition (21) reads 10/19<q<20/21 and holds strictly.
Moreover q<161/200 and
\[
 \left(\frac56\right)^5\frac{135}{133}
    -\left[\left(\frac{161}{200}\right)^5+\frac{25}{399}\right]
 =\frac{2763786689203}{383040000000000}>0.             \tag{23}
\]
Combining (22)-(23) proves that this actual through-centroid cap
has mass STRICTLY LESS THAN Gamma_5 M. Its normalized mass is about
0.384942, whereas Gamma_5 is about 0.401878.

This is a counterexample to transferring the ORDINARY Gamma_d
centroid guarantee to the projected mixed law, with the centroid
still an actual mixed point. It is not an OC counterexample and
does not claim that the true centroid fails the weaker OC target.

Indeed, the own centroid of B_epsilon is an explicit safe candidate
at base 2. Every ambient through-halfspace captures at least
Gamma_5 W V_T from that middle fiber alone; a vertical cap containing
the point captures the whole middle fiber. Its normalized depth is
therefore at least
\[
 \Gamma_5\,\frac W{W+2a}
     =\frac{59375}{157464}
     >\Gamma_5/2.
\]
Thus the source separately satisfies its mixed target.

The verifier checks the repeated-knot endpoint convention, duplicated
moment identities, exact canonical-cap formula in the normal form,
the finite normal-form fiber geometry, and every rational
inequality in this counterexample. The identities above, rather
than a numerical screen, establish the general statements.
